utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll have the first witness. And when that witness has given evidence, we will deal with our rulings in relation to the other witnesses who are on the list about whom rulings are required.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The Prosecution will call as the next witness Mr. Beqe Beqaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Shin, you've got a witness coming?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, what is it, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, just a brief remark, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday, towards the end of the day, towards the end of the hearing, your Registrar gave me papers for K41, a protected witness. (redacted) . Then I saw -- then I saw the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You know quite well that you're not to identify in any way witnesses who are protected. We are dealing with this witness. Mr. Milosevic, you must understand that we cannot deal with administrative matters whenever you want to raise them. They have to be dealt with in an orderly way. Now, we'll deal with your point after we've heard this witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to say a fact to you in relation to this. This name that we got yesterday was mentioned in some electronic media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's deal with it later. Let's deal with this in an orderly way. We'll hear the witness - he's waiting - then you can tell us all that you want to about the other one. Yes. Let's hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If the usher could please place on the ELMO the name of the witness. Thank you. Examined by Mr. Shin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you please tell the Court your full name, first name and last.

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: Beqe Beqaj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you born on the 11th of November 1939 in Racaj village in the municipality of Gjakove?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you are married, had six daughters and two sons, your two sons are still missing, last seen in circumstances described in your evidence?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Beqaj, on the 15th of April, 2000, did you give a statement to a member of the Office of the Prosecutor about the events you witnessed and your experiences in Kosovo during 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 14th of March of this year, did you provide a short addendum to your statement of the 15th of April, 2000?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Beqaj, also on the 14th of March of this year, were you provided with a copy of the statement that you previously gave and a copy of the addendum, both in the Albanian language in the presence of a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor and a presiding officer appointed by the Registrar of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time were you able to confirm that the copy of the statement and the addendum were true and correct?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Beqaj, on Monday, 26th of August, earlier this week, while speaking with myself and other members of the Office of the Prosecutor, did you become aware that there were a few revisions and corrections to be made in your statement? Just yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First, in your statement of the 15th of April, 2000, you say that, reading from the English -- and, Your Honours, this is page 2, second paragraph of that statement -- "In May 1998, the VJ Army and police forces, the MUP, were deployed in the village of Racaj and in other neighbouring villages of the Carragojs Valley." Is that statement correct? And if not, could you please explain very briefly what correction should be made.

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: It's not correct. On the 2nd of August, 1998, Serb forces attacked the villages around Smolica and Junik and the people were forced to abandon their villages, and they set up position after the 2nd of August in the village of Dallashaj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Beqaj. So rather than May 1998 in that sentence, it should say the 2nd of August, 1998; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second, in that same statement, you say that -- referring to events in 1998 - Your Honours, this is the fifth paragraph on page 2 in the English statement: "When we regained possession of our house, I saw that the Serbs had looted our goods. Some of our livestock had been killed. In September 1998, the VJ patrolled all the villages in the valley." Mr. Beqaj, were the livestock referred to in that quotation, were they killed in 1998? And if not, when were they killed?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: There's a change to be made here, too. On the 23rd of March, 1999, around 1.00, Serb forces attacked the village and shot around in the houses and killed the livestock. On the 23rd of March, 1999, not as it is written here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Beqaj. Finally, Mr. Beqaj, when you were leaving Serbia to go to Albania on the 28th of April, 1999, did anything happen to you and others with you leaving Kosovo with regards to identification cards and papers? If so, could you very briefly explain what happened.

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: We had to give up our documents and our passports in the village of Racaj and they wanted them again at the border when we left. And anyone who had documents still had to give them up at the border. And if you didn't have documents, you couldn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Beqaj, who exactly asked you for your documents at the border?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: The police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you yourself provide your documents to the police at the border?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: I had already given up my documents in Racaj when they requested it there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Beqaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, with these revisions and corrections, the Prosecution tenders the two statements into evidence under Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 296.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I will now read a summary of the evidence of Mr. Beqaj. Your Honours, Mr. Beqaj was born in the village of Racaj in Gjakove municipality and was living there at the beginning of 1999. Racaj can be found in the Kosovo atlas on page 9, grid reference G20. Mr. Beqaj gives evidence of deportations from villages north-west of Gjakove during 1998 and 1999 as well as of associated persecutions. He also gives evidence in relation to killings in Meja. In August of 1998, Mr. Beqaj describes that the Yugoslav army and police forces were deployed in the area of the village of Racaj and in other neighbouring villages of the Carragojs Valley. At that time, several men from Racaj were arrested and imprisoned. Also at that time, shooting in the area of Junik and Smolica village caused people from those places to flee towards Racaj. Hearing from those people that the Serb forces were coming to their village, the inhabitants of Racaj, including Mr. Beqaj and his family, escaped towards Gjakove where the witness's family stayed with relatives for five weeks before returning to their village. On the 14th of April, 1999, Mr. Beqaj describes how the VJ and police came again to Racaj, forcing him and his family to leave their house. The entire village of Racaj and other neighbouring villages were expelled at that time, departing in a column of tractors. Houses in Racaj village, including the witness's, were set on fire by the police as the villagers fled. The Serb forces ordered the convoy to go to Albania but via Gjakove and Prizren rather than taking a closer border crossing. En route, an aeroplane dropped bombs that hit the convoy of displaced persons near Bistrazin village, south of Gjakove. A delegation from Belgrade then arrived, taking photos and questioning persons in the convoy. The witness and about 4.000 others who had fled their villages who were there were forced to spend the night in a field. The next day, they were sent back to their villages. As the house of the witness had been burned, he and his family were forced to take shelter in a warehouse on the compound. On the 27th of April, 1999, following the deaths of five MUP officers in the area, Serbian police and VJ soldiers again surrounded the valley and attacked the village of Dobros, where some villagers were killed. Civilians from Dobros fled to Racaj village, these persons telling the inhabitants there that the Serb forces were about to reach Racaj. So the villagers of Racaj, including the witness and his family, once again left their village, travelling in a convoy of tractors, horse carts and cars. This convoy was stopped in Meja at a checkpoint manned by police and VJ soldiers. The police appeared to be leading the operation, Mr. Beqaj explains. Mr. Beqaj states that 24 men were separated from the rest of the convoy and sent to the adjacent meadow where they were forced to sit with their hands behind their heads. All of these 24 men were relatives of Mr. Beqaj, and 13 of them close relatives, including his two sons and two brothers. Mr. Beqaj describes how he also saw 20 other men seated in the field with their hands behind their heads. Mr. Beqaj describes how, when he turned back to see what the police were doing to his relatives, a policeman kicked him and insulted him, accusing him in a general way for the deaths of Serbian policemen and threatening retaliation. The persons still in the convoy, including Mr. Beqaj, were not allowed to look at the men in the meadow. Mr. Beqaj was told to leave together with the convoy. These 24 men have not been seen since then. As the convoy left towards Gjakove, VJ soldiers lined the road. When the convoy reached a school near Meja, they were robbed of their valuables and ID documents by police. Near the school, the witness saw a group of men being lined up, and after awhile, he heard shots. Mr. Beqaj was later told by others that these men had been shot and killed. On the 28th of April, 1999, Mr. Beqaj and his family crossed into Albania. At the border as they were leaving Kosovo, Serbian police officers again demanded any documents from persons in the convoy. That concludes the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say in your statement that on the 2nd of August, 1998, the police arrested 11 men from the village of Racaj and that some of them were released whereas others were kept in detention and taken to the prison in Pec; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your brother was also arrested, and he was released after seven months; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were they arrested?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: You know. You know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you to answer me why they were arrested.

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: They didn't have any -- they weren't guilty of anything. I don't know why they were arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me rephrase the question. Were criminal proceedings instituted against them?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: No. No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. They weren't armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You think they were not armed. I am asking you whether they were armed or whether they were not armed.

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: Some of them may have had something, but your -- your army, when they -- when your army, your forces arrived, they told everyone to give up their arms, and most of the people had given up their arms at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All right. That's when the forces came and asked for their surrender. Out of these 11 who were arrested, how many of them had weapons? When you say some of them had weapons, how many actually did?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: They didn't have arms, but some of the villagers had arms. And when the army came in, they said, "Give up your arms," and some of them gave up their arms at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Beqaj, in your statement you say they had at least one weapon in their houses respectively, at least one weapon. How many weapons did you have in your house?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: Some of the weapons were given up at that time but not all of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many pieces of weapons did you have in your house?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: One. Only one, which was given up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did everybody hand in only one weapon? And you say that they did not hand in everything they had. So whatever they had more than one, they kept?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: No. They didn't have any others. They gave up one weapon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, a little while ago you said that they did not really hand in everything. Isn't that what you said or not?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: I said those who had weapons did give them up. Those who had weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So they just kept something. Tell me, please, Mr. Beqaj --

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was that you were saying?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: They didn't keep any weapons. They gave up everything they had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All right. You say that there was shooting between the army and the KLA in Junik and Smolica; is that right? That's what it says here, in your statement. On the same day, the 2nd of August - that is the third paragraph of the first page of the statement -- it's actually marked as page 2. So on the same day, the 2nd of August, the police and the VJ army were engaged in shootings with the KLA in Junik city and in the village of Smolica, municipality of Gjakove. Now, tell me, since they handed in their weapons, what did they use for shooting at the army and the police? Because you say that everybody handed in their weapons. How come on that day there could be shooting between the army and the police and the KLA if everybody had handed in their weapons?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: I'm talking about my village, not about other villages. I don't know what was going on elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that Smolica and Junik were major strongholds of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that Smolica, in addition to that, was a weapons distribution centre for the arms that were illegally smuggled in from Albania? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: No, I don't know, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who Tahir Zemaj is?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: I don't know him, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. He was a commander there in Smolica. If you don't know him personally, do you know that several hundreds of KLA terrorists and foreign mercenaries in July 1998 entered Yugoslavia illegally from Albania, and he led them then, several hundreds of them. That is an event that I assume you are familiar with. That's June 1998. KLA terrorists and foreign mercenaries, several hundreds of them.

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let us move on, then, to what you were saying yourself. You spent five weeks in Djakovica with some relatives; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you returned to the village and that's when you surrendered your weapons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during those five weeks while you were staying with your relatives in Djakovica, did you have your weapons with you or were the weapons hidden in the house when you returned?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat his answer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're asked to repeat your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were at home. I didn't have them with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, then. How is it possible, then, that, as you said, you returned to the village after you had surrendered your weapons to the Serb forces? If you first handed in your weapons and then returned to your village, how is it possible that the weapons were not on you but were in the village?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: After we went to Gjakove, they contacted certain people who were stationed in Dallashaj and sent the message that anybody who had weapons and handed them in would not be troubled, but it didn't turn out like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You had an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you claim you were not a member of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: I wasn't a member of the KLA. I kept it for my own needs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are one's own needs that need to be achieved with an automatic rifle?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: To protect myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To protect yourself against whom?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: From your army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for how long had you had owned that rifle?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: I don't really remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know for how long you had that rifle. Well, how did you obtain it?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: From the army. I got it from the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: No. I bought it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, you bought it. Well, please make yourself clear. Did you obtain it or did you buy it?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: I bought it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much did you pay for it?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: That's my business.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. That's an answer too. Did you personally hand over your rifle to the police?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you said some people had at least one rifle, how many locals had more than one rifle of various -- or, rather, various types of weapons?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: I don't know. Several of them handed them in, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the possession of automatic weapons - that's a military type of weapon, an automatic weapon - that that was a crime?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: I don't know, but the officer came and took them by truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They collected so many in trucks. There were so many of these weapons that they had to use trucks to collect them. How many weapons were collected on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter requests the witness to repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're asked to repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This person said to me that -- the person said it was forbidden to carry arms, but he had them by themselves in trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You said that between September 1998 and March 1999 - that's virtually throughout the period of the presence of the Verification Mission in Kosovo - together with others from the village, you were hiding in the woods; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: Would you ask the question again? I didn't understand it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated in your statement, Mr. Beqaj, that between September 1998 and March 1999, which means throughout that period, together with other men of the village, were in hiding in the hills; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: That's right. The army, after sending us back to the village and telling us that nobody would bother us, the police were patrolling round there and asking for the young men. And when they came to arrest people with their patrols, we had to flee and go to the hills.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me with whom you were hiding in the hills.

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: I wasn't hiding, but whenever the police came, I had to go and hide in the hills because otherwise they would arrest me and put me in prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. How large was that group? How many of you were there hiding in the hills?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: It wasn't a group. Everybody ran away by themselves to get away from the police, because otherwise they would end up in prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you did have weapons, you were hiding in the hills, but you were not members of the KLA. You were fleeing the police so as not to be sent to prison, and you are claiming that you were not a member of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: I say that I'm not a member of the KLA and -- and we surrendered our weapons to you, not to the KLA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. During that period of time while you were hiding in the hills, that is between September 1998 and March 1999, were there any shootings, as you mentioned here, between the KLA and the army and the police?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: No. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You said that on the 14th of April, you were forced to leave your home and to go to Albania. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were you forced to leave your house and go to Albania?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: On the 14th of April, at 9.00 in the morning, the soldiers and policemen came in an operation and forced us to go to Albania as soon as possible. We had to get out with our tractors, cars, carts, whatever means of transport people had. And while we were leaving the village, we saw the houses being burned. And we were forced out by your army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you telling us that there was no fighting between the KLA and the army or the police but that the army just came in just like that, walked into the village and told you, "Go to Albania"? Is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: The police and the army came and told us to leave the village at once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Beqaj, is it true that you were actually leaving the village to take shelter from the conflict that was going on? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: No. We were forced out. It wasn't fighting at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So you were not fleeing the war, but you left because you were told to go. Were you in the column that was shelled near the village of Bistrazin?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: Bishtazhin. Yes, I was there. In a column of tractors, I was in front, and there was a villager from Racaj behind me. And they struck the tractor and killed 11 of them on this tractor, besides others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among others. And how many in total were killed in that bombing operation near the village of Bistrazin?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: About 75.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the NATO planes as they were approaching to bomb the column? Or was visibility good? Was it a clear day?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: We saw the planes but we didn't recognise them as NATO planes. They were Serbian planes. And they bombed us, but they were low. They weren't very high.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Okay. You don't have to go into that explanation. We've heard that already. Tell me, please, is it true that the army and the police extended aid to all the wounded and drove them to hospital?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they did not transport the wounded to hospital. What happened to the wounded? Who helped them then?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know who transported them. I have no knowledge of this. As long as -- they remained there as long as I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you said that you were forced to spend the night in Bistrazin. So you were there all night. Who forced you to spend the night there?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: The police stayed with us the whole night until the morning at 4.00. Then they came from Belgrade and they photographed us, and they questioned some people and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that was an investigation into the bombing incident and the killing of so many people by NATO. Is that clear or not? Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: They asked questions, but who they were, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But tell me, did you see and notice foreign journalists present, filming the incident, both domestic and foreign reporters? Did you see TV crews? Did you see photographers? Did you see all these people who had come from Belgrade, representatives of foreign and domestic media? Did you see those people?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: They were there with video cameras, and they asked questions, and they were Serbs. But I don't know about anybody else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on from that event. We certainly don't have too much time. You said that a policeman, Vojo Pekovic, was killed. In the fourth paragraph of page 3. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you say that three days later, in the village of Meja, another policeman was killed called Milutin; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No killed those policemen?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you learn of the killing of those policemen?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: People knew. People during the journey, they found out by accident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they tell you that your terrorists from the KLA had done it in an ambush?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: What kind of terrorists?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The KLA.

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: That's not right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who, then, could have killed those police officers?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, you are aware of the fact that in Bistrazin, during the bombing operation, dozens of people were killed. A moment ago you said 75. The number isn't important now, I'm not asking you about that number. Also near the village of Meja, a column was bombed, a column of Albanians, again by NATO. So Meja and Bistrazin are well-known locations where a large number of Albanians were killed by NATO. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was from NATO, but I know that it was from planes. There was. They were flying very low.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Planes. In Meja and Bistrazin. And also in the Carragojs Valley, which goes on from Meja, and in that whole area there was fierce fighting between the army and the police on the one hand and the KLA on the other. And this went on for several days. Do you know of that? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: That's not true. What they call the Carragojs Valley has 12 villages, including all the villages round the border were emptied by your army. And in the end, they captured 500 people in the village of Meja-Orize and in Korenica. 500 people went away that day and never returned, and nobody knows where they are today. You know where they are today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know how many policemen and soldiers of the Yugoslav army were killed in those combat operations in the Carragojs Valley that you have mentioned, saying that there were 12 villages there? So how many were killed fighting with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: That's right. The KLA never fought in the Carragojs Valley ever. The army emptied all the villages round the border because it was a security zone. And then they took, as I said, 500 people, and they -- all trace of them was lost and -- from that day on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You don't have to repeat that. You've told us that. But what do you think? How did those numerous soldiers and police officers get killed if nobody shot at them?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: It's not ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who killed those soldiers and policemen?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: It's very hard for me to say this, but this is not true at all. Nobody was killed at all. Not a single was killed in the Carragojs Valley, and there was no fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We have had witnesses testifying about that, so I won't ask you any more questions about that. Unfortunately for your side, it was an Albanian, an officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's all comment. Now, anything more for this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do have quite a number of questions. About ten more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are claiming that the army separated 24 men?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: I said that my four brothers, we don't know about their whereabouts to this date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, is it true that you are saying that they separated 24 men?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on that same page, in paragraph 3, you say that you didn't see the army pointing their weapons at those men.

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: That's not true. What do you mean I didn't see it? I was there. I had my hands tied before my -- behind my back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were tied as well?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: No, I wasn't tied. I wasn't tied. But they were separating them, and they were forcing them to put their hands behind their heads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please. Let me read out a part of your statement from page 4 to you. "On the left-hand side of the road in the direction of Korenica I saw ten people lined up on the field. I was at a distance of about 100 metres. I could see well and I did not see soldiers pointing guns at the men. I passed by that place and I headed towards Djakovica. After awhile, I heard shootings. Later, when we were on the way to Albania, somebody told me that these men who were lined up near the school had been seen when they fell on the ground." Is that what you know about those men? And on the basis of what somebody told you on the way to Albania, that people were seen falling on the ground, you are claiming that those people were executed and shot?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: I will repeat once again what I've said before. I've seen --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't need to repeat what you said before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let him explain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is as it was. At one -- at a distance of 100 metres, I've seen those men standing, and it is right. I didn't see automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You go further than that and say: "I cannot say anything more specific as to where the shooting came from," that you heard later on as you were going towards Djakovica, "because there was shooting throughout the area." That means, as you are claiming, that there was shooting all over the place and you can't tell where exactly the shooting was coming from. So if that is so, was it clear to you at the time that there was fighting going on, a conflict of some sorts?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: That was the firing of your police and your army, because we were all surrounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, Mr. Beqaj, is it clear to you that these localities where NATO killed the largest number of Albanians, through these rumours, "I heard, I was told," and so on, you are endeavouring to transform into locations where crimes were committed by members of the army of Yugoslavia or the police, which is not true. Is that your intention?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: Who took 500 persons? Where are they? Could you please tell me that? Where are they?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Beqaj, what is being suggested is that you made all this up. Now, is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The accused is saying that you have made all this up. Now, is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I have not made this up. I was there and I am testifying here about things that I have seen myself with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, then. Mr. Beqaj, you didn't see any of these things you are testifying about. You did not witness any executions by shooting. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: That's right. I did not see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, you're testifying about something that you did not observe, and you're admitting now that you didn't see it. Now, please explain something to me which is not clear, at the end of your statement. This is third from the bottom at the very end of the statement. You are describing what these members of what you call a Serbian paramilitary group looked like, and in the last sentence, you said: "They left the place when the jeep started approaching." "They left the place when the jeep was approaching us." Who was approaching? What kind of a jeep was approaching? What was actually happening? Could you explain this, please, because it's not clear from the statement.

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I will explain. While we were heading towards Krushe e Madhe, on our way to Albania, two soldiers met us. They were armed. They had hand grenades hanging on their belts and in their hands, and they were threatening us. They wanted to loot us. They asked for money. And then two police jeeps - I think they were police jeeps, I'm not sure - two police jeeps came and then I guess they were scared and ran away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So you described the following event; that some robbers, who exist in any war, and that is not being denied, who wanted to rob you ran away when a police jeep approached you and now you say it was two police jeeps. So, is it clear to you that these robbers do not belong either to the army or to the police, that these are simple highwaymen?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: They were in military clothes. I don't know who they were, but they were in military clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What people can wear in times of war is a different matter altogether, but you are saying yourself that they ran away from the police. There was probably a reason why they fled from the police. They are trying to rob someone and then they run away when a police vehicle comes up. That is what you've been saying. But, all right, let us move on. I just have a few more questions. In the village of Meja, in addition to this Serb policeman, do you know that the KLA also killed three Albanians who were loyal citizens of the Republic of Serbia? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know the fact at all that the KLA killed many Albanians who respected the state, the Republic of Serbia, and behaved like normal peace-loving citizens? The KLA. The Albanians killed them, a large number. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that you went to Albania on the 28th of April. How many of you were there in that group when you crossed the border?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: The convoy consisted of hundreds of people. I don't know the exact number, but it was a big convoy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you use to cross the border?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: I was on a horse cart, as I mentioned it before, and there were some children on the way who were not able to walk, and we placed them in the cart and took them with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But for the most part, people were on tractors, not on horse carts. Tractors and trucks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: Some on tractors, some on foot. There were even people on foot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, why do you say that documents were taken away from you at the border, that they were burned, and so on? Yesterday we saw a film here where Albanians, not towards the end of April but towards the end of May in Albania --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: In Pristina, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- are getting new passports, travelling buses, normal bus lines. Who told you to tell this story that documents were taken away from you and that your things were taken away from you? Explain that to me, please.

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: The road that takes to Korenica, as soon as you get to the asphalt road, there was blanket that they had placed there, and they would say, like, "Put your documents, your money, personal documentation, everything you have on these blankets."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this better be your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make all of this up, Mr. Beqaj?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: What do you mean, "Did you make this up?" I don't understand your question. I did not make anything up. I am talking of things that I've seen myself. I didn't make anything up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did somebody else invent this for you and tell you to say it?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: I wasn't told by anyone. I have went through this experience, and I've experienced it myself, and I will never forget it to the end of my life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Mr. Tapuskovic. No. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there are no questions for Witness Beqaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Any re-examination? Re-examined by Mr. Shin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Beqaj, when you were forced to leave, you and your family, your village on the 14th of April, 1999, you say that houses were being burned in your village. At that time or later, did you discover how many houses were burned in your village, and if so, how many were burned, approximately, please?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: As we were fleeing, as soon as we left the village, we saw the houses on fire. And when we returned, 80 per cent of the houses were burnt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you and your family and the other villagers returned to Racaj, did any authorities - police, army, or any other authorities - offer any assistance to you or your family?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone from the Serbian police come to investigate the burning of some 80 per cent of the houses in your village?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mention in your statement that the police asked for your identity documents and valuables to be placed on this blanket near this intersection near Meja-Orize. Did the persons who asked you this, did they explain why your identification cards or indeed your valuables were required to be handed over to them?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: They said, "Give us your documents, because you don't need your documents any more. You are on your way to Albania." And they took our money as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please describe for us the uniforms that these persons who asked for your identification and valuables, the uniforms they were wearing.

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: They were wearing police uniforms. They were police camouflaged uniforms. It was the police who requested our documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what colour were their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: BEQE BEQAJ
utterances.text: Like the police uniforms; camouflaged greenish uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Beqaj, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask a question, please? This is a request, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, if you'd ask it very shortly. We don't usually allow witnesses to make any speeches, but you can ask a question, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm requesting from The Hague Tribunal and the international community to shed some light on the disappearance of 500 people. We don't know where they are, and Milosevic must know it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we can't take any cognisance of that final comment of yours about the accused but what you say about the 500 people is, of course, noted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will deal with the administrative matters. Mr. Ryneveld, we have applications in relation to, I think, seven witnesses in front of us. They are all for evidence to be admitted under Rule 92 bis. There is Mr. Milaim Cekaj. He gives evidence as a prisoner from Dubrava, and he deals with the NATO bombing and the alleged executions. Next, Mr. Ismet Haxhiavdija. He deals with the murders in Milosh Gilic Street and Djakovica. Mr. Behar Haxhiavdija similarly. Mr. Gani Bacaj, again a prisoner in Dubrava who gives evidence about matters there. Mr. Izet Krasniqi, who deals with the attack on the convoy at Studime e Poshtme. Ms. Sofije Imeraj, who deals with the murders as alleged in the Imeraj part of Padaliste. And Mr. Mehdi Gerguri, who also deals with the attack on the convoy at Studime e Poshtme. Now, all those are cumulative in the sense that evidence about those matters has been given before. We would be minded to admit them under Rule 92 bis. We'll, of course, hear from the accused first. Is there anything in addition you want to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. As you have indicated, they are cumulative in nature and that is our proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you've heard what's said. We're considering the admissibility of the evidence of those seven witnesses under Rule 92 bis, subject to cross-examination by yourself. We know what your standard objection is. You've referred to it before. That is, you object to any evidence in written form. We know that. Is there anything that you wish to add about these particular witnesses?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing to add. I have the same objection, so I don't want to take up any more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll admit the statements, subject to cross-examination. Now, there was some point that you wanted to make earlier, Mr. Milosevic. It may be sensible, since it's about -- it seems to be about a protected witness, if we go into private session. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to raise the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You may not want to. We'll go into private session and we'll hear what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. In light of the ruling with respect to the 92 bis, I propose to call Milaim Cekaj as our next witness. He does give evidence about Dubrava prison. While the witness is being brought in, might I refresh Your Honours' memory that the Kosovo atlas, page 5, at the intersection of block J at the top and 12 down the side, shows Dubrava about six or seven kilometres to the east of Istok.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Examined by Mr. Ryneveld:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cekaj, I understand, sir, that you are a 35-year-old Kosovar Albanian Muslim from the municipality of Decani in the west of Kosovo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you hold an agricultural engineering degree, you're married, you now have two young sons and a daughter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also true, sir, that you carried out your compulsory military service in the engineering branch of the Yugoslav army in 1985 and 1986?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And is it also true, sir, that you joined the KLA in early April 1998 and as such you were an instructor of arms, weapons and training and were in charge of a company; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, following the events in -- that transpired in Kosovo in 1999, did you give a statement to members of the Office of the Prosecutor on the 17th of May of the year 2000?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And subsequent to that, sir, have you had an opportunity to refresh your memory from that statement in Albanian and appear before a presiding officer of this Tribunal and acknowledge to that presiding officer that the contents of your statement were true and accurate to the best of your knowledge, information, and belief?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that occurred on the 26th of August this year, 2002; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I propose at this point to read a brief summary and then ask the witness a couple of questions and show him the aerial photograph of Dubrava that's been entered as an exhibit. Your Honours, very briefly, the witness, I understand from the statement, was arrested on the 28th of October, 1998, by Serb police and a military officer and then taken to the Peja police station. At the police station, the witness was interrogated for two days by up to eight members of the state police. He was beaten and forced to sign a 15-page document in Serbian that proved ultimately to be a confession. He was then detained in the Peja gaol at the rear of the police station until the 19th of February, 1999, in terrible conditions. On the 2nd and 3rd of November, 1998, the witness was taken to Peja court where he was questioned by the investigating judge, Milomir Lazovic; and on the 19th of February, 1999, the witness, along with about 50 to 60 other prisoners, was transferred from Peja gaol to Dubrava Prison. Here, the witness was put into cellblock 48 on the upper floor of the C2 block referred, if you recall the Exhibit 289, as the isolations block. In his statement, he names his fellow cellmates and he alleges that the beating of prisoners by the guards was a daily occurrence. They were locked up 24 hours a day with no exercise. Well, on the 19th of May, 1999 NATO bombed Dubrava Prison. During his proofing session, the witness advised that the first bomb struck building C1. He advised that C1 in 1998 served as a weapons and munitions warehouse for the Serbian forces. The rest of the prison had been their logistics headquarters between March and September of 1998. During that period, the prisoners had been transferred to other prisons. Dubrava reopened as a prison for Albanian prisoners in early December 1998. And you will recall that the last witness to talk about Dubrava testified that he was transferred there on the 5th of December. Anti-aircraft guns near the prison, outside the perimeter wall, shot at NATO planes on a nearly daily basis prior to the bombing. On the 19th of May as well, one bomb struck the cellblock in which he was located, killing three prisoners. He gives the surname of one of those killed as Topalli. The witness then describes an additional, more prolonged NATO attack on the 21st of May, 1999, when he saw planes bomb the heating plant, the administration building, kitchen, theatre, and other buildings inside the prison compound. One rocket or bomb which missed the theatre, killed 18 or 19 prisoners. The witness names two of those killed in his statement, and he indicated during proofing that 23 prisoners in total were killed by NATO bombing over that two-day bombing period. In the early morning of the 22nd of May, 1999, the prisoners were instructed to line up near the watchtower by guards on the pretext that they were going to be transferred to Nis prison in Serbia. In his statement, he indicates that guards with bazooka-like weapons known as Zolja, automatic weapons, mortar projectiles, rifle grenades, and hand grenades then fired upon the prisoners. The witness was wounded by grenade fragments. During a lull in the shooting, the witness took the opportunity to run to his cellblock. Snipers in the various watchtowers continued to shoot at the prisoners after the main firing had ceased. In so doing, killing more prisoners. Later in the afternoon, the witness saw eight soldiers in green camouflage uniforms enter the compound and kill prisoners in the reception block of the compound. He names two prisoners killed. On the 23rd of May, at around 5.00, the witness, who was tending to the wounded, saw men inside the compound wearing olive-coloured uniforms with "Milicija" written on the back, and blue uniforms and green camouflage uniforms with white wolf-head badges with "Vukovi" written beneath. These men threw hand grenades into drains and buildings where prisoners were hiding, and fired automatic guns at them. The prisoners were ordered to surrender, after which they were taken to the gymnasium. The witness assisted in taking injured prisoners to the gymnasium and then hid in a cellblock. After about an hour, he emerged on seeing prisoners walking freely around the compound. At the sports field, the scene of the previous day's killings, the witness saw more than 150 corpses. He recognised three of the dead whom he names. On the 24th of May, the following day, the witness and all the remaining prisoners, including the wounded, were transferred to Lipjan prison by bus and truck. And on the 10th of June, the witness was transferred from Lipjan to Pozharevc prison. While in that prison, he was charged with organising terrorism based on that confession he was forced to sign in Peja and was ultimately sentenced to 18 months imprisonment and was released on the 26th of April, 2000. He also, of course, describes prison officials, including the director of the Dubrava Prison, and he also provides an additional aerial photograph of Dubrava Prison, indicating locations mentioned in his statement. Now, could Exhibit 289 very briefly be shown to the witness and put on the ELMO. And while we're doing that, Madam Registrar, I neglected to ask you for the number for the bis package, and I haven't -- it hasn't been distributed. I'm aware of the time. I'll do this in one minute, if I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 297.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cekaj, looking at the photograph that's now on the ELMO, could you take a pen and indicate to us very, very briefly, first of all, the cellblock where you were detained when you arrived at the prison. Mark it.

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: This was C2 block. I was in this room number 43, where the window is, you can see here, and that is room 47.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Moving over to the sports field, is the watchtower shown in this photograph, and if not, where is it in relation to the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: You can't see the watchtower in this photograph, which is opposite the sports field, but it was -- it was round about here. Here's the external wall, and those two walls meet at this point off the edge, and that's where the watchtower is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And where were the men asked to line up? Could you just point that out?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: Yes. I say that the watchtower was over here, and that early in the morning --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You will have to put your -- for the record, you're now indicating an area off the screen to the bottom right-hand corner of the photograph; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: You can't see it here, but they ordered us -- just a moment. They ordered us, first of all, to line up in fours, and after a time, he said -- he said to us in Serbian, "Line up," and the line was from there to there. So that is facing up to the watchtower.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The watchtower's not visible. Were the lines facing the watchtower, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: Yes, they were facing because that was what the order was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One more question. Where did the shooting come from? Can you point that out on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: Yes. The shots first came from outside the wall, because in all probability, they used hand grenades and hand-held rocket launchers. And then they came from the watchtower where there were people with Zoljas. And there were also people with machine-guns -- with eight millimetre machine-guns, which are also called ubiza [phoen], and they were standing on their feet and they would fire these machine-guns from that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what -- if you could use the pointer, show the Judges, if you would, please, where the shooting was coming from in relation to where the prisoners were.

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: The prisoners were lined up that way, and the shots came from the watchtower and from behind the wall. I should emphasise because it's very important, that the wall was damaged at this point. There was a hole of about 20 centimetres wide. And this was about 70 centimetres above the ground. And while they -- while we were lining up, I saw people on the other side of the wall through that hole, and you could see the barrels of semi-automatic and machine-guns through that hole.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Those are my questions at this point, thank you, Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 9152 to 9159. Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are going to adjourn now, Mr. Cekaj. Could you remember not to speak to anybody about your evidence during the adjournment until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution. We're going to adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You graduated from the agriculture faculty in Pristina, as I understand it. Is that at the regular Pristina University?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As an Albanian, did you have any kind of problems at the university while you were a student and when you graduated in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: Of course I had problems, because, like all the other faculties at Prishtina University, the agricultural faculty had the same fate after your regime occupied the university premises and threw out the teachers and students. So I -- I completed part of my studies in the joint university, and I completed my studies in premises that weren't intended to be used for study, but I completed it in the Albanian language.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How could you study if you say that the Albanian students were thrown out of the university?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: They were expelled from their proper premises, thanks to your regime, after 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you study up to 1995? When did you start your studies?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: After being expelled from the proper premises of the agricultural faculty - I don't know how relevant this is - I was with my parents in Germany for a time, and then the education was put straight in a kind of way thanks to the voluntary contributions of the Albanians themselves and no thanks to the regime of that time. And then the faculties started working again, and I completed my fourth year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the agricultural faculty, like the other faculties at Pristina University, never stopped operating, that they were working normally throughout?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: I know, but once I had the honour of going to this faculty which you say didn't stop work at all, and I was stopped by the police and I was met by policemen, and I was threatened and mistreated, and that was simply when I went to go and get a certificate of my marks of the courses I'd completed. So there was just no place for Albanians there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, come on. You're not going to tell us that there were policemen standing around the faculties, letting people in and out. You know that was never the case.

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: I know that they were not only there but they were at every other faculty. And just to illustrate this, I can tell you that at -- for instance, at the medical faculty, the dean of that time, as you know very well, or you should know if you don't, they threw the dean out from his own office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I think we've done enough on education. Let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. It is very important for the credibility of the witness for us to hear these untruths, of which there are many in his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were a member of the KLA as of April 1998, and a moment ago, in the course of the examination-in-chief, unless it was misquoted in the transcript, you said that you became a member somewhat earlier. When did you join the KLA? If I remember well, it said here 1996 or 1997, whereas in your statement it says in 1998. Which is the correct date?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: Before answering this question about the KLA, I want to say that I didn't tell lies, but I will answer you now. And there's data from the time to show that I'm telling the truth. And I would ask the Court not to interrupt me with insults, otherwise I will return with the same coin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Cekaj, I know this is an emotional business, giving evidence, and I know that it's a strain. The accused is under control. He knows full well the questions he can ask and those that he can't, but he is entitled to ask questions. He is on trial and, therefore, he must be allowed to test the witness's evidence. Now, it will be for the Court to decide whether the questions are relevant or not, and it would be better if, instead of arguing with him, you remember that you are giving evidence to a Court, and could you address us and just answer the questions as best you can. If you can't answer a question, just say that, "I can't answer," tell us why not, and we will decide how to take the matter forward. But do not be offended by the allegations made by the accused. He's entitled to make them. It will be for us to decide whether there's anything in them or not. We'll get on more quickly if you just concentrate on the questions and answer them as briefly as you can. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. The same goes for you: Don't argue with the witness or otherwise you're wasting a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I just might. I believe that the witness was reacting to the suggestion that there were untruths in his statement. That, I think, is what prompted the outburst.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I simply -- I realise and -- that Your Honours, and I will answer every question. But as for the second question -- or the first question about the KLA, it's true that I was involved in the KLA from April 1998. And the other dates that the accused has mentioned have -- I have not said in anything that I have said or written that I was involved in 1996 or 1997. That's been mixed up somehow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I asked you from when you were a member. You said 1998 and that's sufficient. You were a commander of a unit and an instructor for weapons for a district consisting of 13 villages; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: I was -- I simply served in my own village, which is called Irzniq. I don't know how these 13 villages came up, but it is true that Irzniq is a local community that does include 13 villages. And all the young men of these villages completed this training that I mentioned in my village. And the other data are all in the statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which unit were you in command of?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: I was also a company commander in the village where three companies were organised; 1, 2, 3. I was the commander of the 1st Company, and before that, as I mentioned in my statement, I was involved in the training of the young men with weapons and -- and you know what training involves. In other words, physical fitness, technical -- technical exercises, other technical things involving weapons and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, how many men did this unit of which you were the commander have? You describe it as a company. What was its strength?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: During the training, there was above -- there were more than 145.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, please, what kind of weapons was the unit armed with?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: All the conventional weapons that belong to a company. They had them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is included under conventional weapons that belong to a company? Could you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I can explain. We had anti-tank weapons, that is, hand-held mortars. We had machine-guns of 12.7 millimetre and 8 millimetre calibre, and ordinary infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you consider, under "normal infantry weapons" that every soldier should have an automatic weapon; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: At the first -- at first, we didn't have this, we didn't have this kind of weapon, but later this situation improved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. From April, as it says here, in 1998, you held that position. And in how many attacks against the army and the police and the citizens did your company take part in in the summer and autumn of 1998, and in which attacks?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: Rather than say "attack," I would say "defence operation," because we didn't go anywhere up to Smadija [phoen] or Pozharevc in Serbia. We were only defending our own territory and our own homes and our own positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, in which conflicts, if you wish to call them that, did you take part, together with your unit, against the police and army?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: If you need this information, you should take it from the operations rooms of your units. But whenever we were attacked, we defended ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many defence operations you were involved in, Mr. Cekaj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Depends, because we had a kind of schedule, and depending on the schedule allocated to me whenever I was on duty or whenever there was a serious danger, I was involved. Even when I was on leave, I would take part. A kind of -- it was a kind of leave that really I deserved, but I don't really know the numbers of these operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there many battles that you were involved in?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many Serbs did you kill, you personally?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: I have -- I didn't kill Serbs. I was merely involved in fighting. And in war, you don't know. So in this sense, "how many you killed," I understand that as execution, and I haven't executed anybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many Serbs, Albanians, and others did you kill?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: I am here to tell the truth, and I'm on oath, and I will tell this truth again. I can -- that is that the KLA, and I can say this in full sense of responsibility, was one of the cleanest armies that never killed civilians, either Albanians or Serbs. And this is documented. And from the beginning of July, I was on the way through some villages, and I was -- I saw various pigs in a yard, and I asked my -- and I asked my driver, "How does this Muslim village have pigs?" And he said, "This is Tresko's [phoen] house." I don't know his surname, but I know that he was commander of the police station in Decan, and he had his house entirely intact with all its infrastructure, and his doors were there, open, just as in normal circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please try and answer my questions. My question was: How many people did you kill in 1998, that is, in the summer and the autumn, how many people did you kill together with your unit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He has said that they killed no civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many soldiers and policemen did you kill?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: I don't know. It was difficult to tell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the problem. Is that why you were arrested by the police and transferred to the investigating prison in Dubrava?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: At first I was arrested and I was held for four months in Peja and about 84 days in isolation in number 13 where the conditions were terrible, and then one month in room number 3 in Peja. And on the 11th of February, I was transferred to Dubrava Prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of the investigations procedure and at the court later in Leskovac, at the District Court in Leskovac, you did not admit to what you are telling us you did now. And as you have just told us, you were even the commander of that unit, and you were involved in those terrorist activities against the legal organs, that is the police and the army. So you were sentenced for only the acts that were proven; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: You mentioned the investigative procedure, but you know very well because you are a lawyer yourself, you know what an investigative procedure is. And as for the investigating judge, Milomir Lazovic, I defended myself by remaining silent. And as for the judgement in Leskovac, the guards - and you can find out their names - and the lawyer, I don't know how it can be called a trial when the guards were sitting next to me on left and right and threatening me all the time and saying that they would gouge my eyes out and slit my throat if I didn't confess to the accusation. So let's not even mention the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You yourself said a moment ago that you took part in armed conflicts with the army and the police. You were arrested and convicted to a term of one and a half years, and you don't even know how many people you've killed. And you consider that an injustice was done. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: Let me draw a suitable parallel between yourself and myself and how we are being treated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think we get anywhere by this. Mr. Milosevic, he's dealt with this point. There's no point arguing about it. We know what happened. We've got his account of the trial. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know of the criminal act for which you were sentenced to a year and a half, according to the Criminal Code of Yugoslavia, the punishment can be up to 15 years of imprisonment?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: That's not true, and I'm sorry that you should mention this as a lawyer, that clauses 115, 125 provide up to 15 years in prison. And 125 and 133 mention up to 20 years in prison, because -- but if you're exaggerating things, you know what this means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you consider that you received a mild sentence for the act you committed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, of course he thinks it's an injustice. But what's -- it's of no relevance here. All that matters is what actually happens. His feelings about it, I'm afraid, are not relevant to these proceedings or, indeed, to your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What feelings, Mr. May? What feelings? From the end of the summer recess, you're bringing to the witness box terrorists and killers. It's a disgrace for Western justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you got any more questions for this witness? Well, then, get on and ask them. No, Mr. Cekaj, don't you join in. Just let's get on. Now, the cross-examination of this witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were beaten and that four days after that, you find yourself facing a judge. If you were really beaten up, then this must have been visible.

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, why did you make this up? Four days later, your injuries must have been visible in court.

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: It would confirm of this. This would be best to contact the warden of Peja prison, who examined my state of health. And as for things being visible in front of investigative judge, everything was so mixed up there you couldn't tell who was the judge and who were the guards and who were the bodyguards. It was a very confused procedure. And I received -- as for receiving a mild sentence, I received a rather heavy one and also had to pay a lot of money in hard currency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, you had to pay money? Mr. Cekaj, it says here that you requested the presence of your attorney, an Albanian, Adem Gorani, and you said that that is why the hearing was postponed, and that he was present the next day.
