So in your file there is no objection on your part or your lawyer that someone beat you. And as you know, that also is a criminal act. Therefore, how can you explain that you are now claiming that someone beat you when you had an attorney who surely would have made such an objection if you yourself did not remember to do so?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: There were a lot of appeals at that time. And besides what you call the legal authorities, headed by yourself, there were also other channels which took money and were involved in filthy business. And the chairman of the Peja court was involved in this and so were his henchmen. And the same was true in Leskovac and Kraljevo, Nis, and other places. You know this very well. You know how matters were done at that time. It happened in Pozharevc too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know very well that it is impossible for prisoners to be beaten in prison, and I know very well that your attorney that you brought to court would certainly have had to make written submissions in court about that if that were true. So I know that very well. As for what you are saying, let me quote your judgement.

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: No. There was no -- not only a possibility of being beaten but of being killed, because more than 150 prisoners were beaten, and I've forgotten the beatings by now. They were not only beaten but murdered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. That is what you are claiming.

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: It's not what I'm claiming, it is the truth, the hard truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In connection what you mentioned, a very large sum of money, you were sentenced - and I have your judgement here - to a prison term of one year and six months, including the time spent in detention. And on -- in the name of expenses of the court, you're expected to pay 1.000 dinars, or the equivalent of 30 German marks, to make it clear to those present, and also a lump sum of 5.000 dinars, which is about 120 German marks, and all within a time limit of 15 days. Those are those enormous fines that you mention as being part of your punishment. Also there is the judgement of the Supreme Court which rejected the appeal of the prosecutor to increase your sentence and the appeal of the Defence counsel to reduce your sentence. And that is how it was. Is that true, Mr. Cekaj?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: It is not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you want to say something, Mr. Cekaj, you can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I talk with him in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. The point is you're giving evidence here, not arguing with him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, he's put to you that there were fines, he's put the figures to you, and he's also put the conviction. Now, if there's something you want to say about that, you can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, yes. I mentioned dollars, marks. I didn't mention dinars. And I don't know how that was translated. This is a matter of your interpreters. But first I had to pay $10.000, and then about 15.000 marks later on, in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Who did you have to pay those sums to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the henchmen of the courts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since this is an obvious situation of the witness not telling the truth, I would like to have this judgement exhibited. I would like to tender it into evidence because it says exactly what his conviction is in terms of the time he's supposed to serve and also the fine he's supposed to pay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the judgement can be exhibited, if you hand it in, subject to any objection in due course, when the Prosecution have had a chance to read it. Now, I suggest that we move on. You have got a quarter of an hour left for your cross-examination. If you challenge the witness's evidence about the executions which he's described at Dubrava, you should do so now, and if you want to ask him about the bombing there. You have a quarter of an hour to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that I have a bit more time, Mr. May, because the other side did not examine him for the prescribed five minutes but much longer. I assumed that you are not going to restrict me either. Let me move on to Dubrava immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Since you raised it, you will have the usual time, and that is until 11.45.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I need a clarification, there are two documents and they're both --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: There are two documents and they're both in B/C/S. Shall we give one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Give them the same number, A and B.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: They will be marked D33A, and D33B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You have been saying that anti-aircraft guns that were shooting at NATO aeroplanes - and I'm reading from your statement - were one or two kilometres away from the prison, and you say, "Once or twice I saw a trail of smoke of the bombs that were fired by the aircraft." So if these aircraft were two kilometres away from the prison, what did they have to do with the prison itself?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: I don't know -- I don't know about the definition of one or two kilometres, but I said in my statement that anti-aircraft artillery was used from positions of your forces outside the wall nonstop. From the first day of the NATO bombardment to the critical day of 19th, 20th, and the 21st, 23rd. I didn't say up to two kilometres, but I mentioned on the first photograph that my windows looked towards the wall in room 48 on the left hand wing of block C2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Give shorter answers to my questions because I'm quoting your very own statement. I'm not making any assumptions. I just asked you what kind -- what anything had to -- what any position of an anti-aircraft unit had to do, if it was two kilometres away from the prison, with the prison itself? You're an instructor for weapons, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: It's very important because they didn't have enough space there, so they had a space where they could carry out their operations, not be right next to the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All right. You were in block C2; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it says here bombs reached the ground floor. You were on the first floor of C2; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: Yes. In the middle of block C2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The bombs had come all the way to the ground floor, and it is your claim that only three men lost their lives. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: Yes. That's very true, because the bombs fell in the middle of the block, just by the warden's room. This was a room which was used for television, and there were 20 prisoners inside, and it exploded and many were injured and killed. And besides this, the bombs fell in the left-hand side in the corridor. Fortunately, they fell in the corridor. And they destroyed the ceiling because it was a concrete construction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understood that, but could you please just give me shorter answers. They then allowed you to go to the school block, to remain in corridors so that you would not be locked up. They said to you and to -- that God should help both you and them, and that you could move about freely within the compound.

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: Just one detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One important detail which you're overlooking no doubt on purpose. After we had broken some of the doors, which took about 40 minutes or an hour, we went out into the yard and then Miloljub Vidic came out to us with his team and ordered us to sit down among -- opposite C1, at one end of C1, at the open space.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. It seems to me that whatever question I put to you, you give me such long explanations that I can only put very few questions to you. Please. You wrote here, when speaking about the 21st of May: "After that, all buildings were hit within the prison compound. That is to say all buildings within the prison compound were hit. One rocket or bomb, which was obviously intended to hit the theatre, missed and then on the spot 18 or 19 prisoners were killed." And then you say who was among the killed persons. Among these 19 or 18 prisoners that you saw who were killed at a seven-metre distance, that is what you actually saw. And at the same time, you say that bombs hit all the buildings of the prison. So you could not see how many people were killed in all the buildings within the prison. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: Look --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I say is it right or is it not right?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: I have to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Pause. Let the witness answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it not the way you wrote it here?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: Your Honour, he is overlooking a very important ingredient on purpose and that is the moment when we left C2 block. When Dragan Milunovic came and threatened us. You asked for a republic and little Aca, his assistant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let him finish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd take care of you tonight if I had the order --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It doesn't pertain to my question at all.

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: It may seem unbelievable, but that rocket hit seven to eight metres, and that's what the distance of the crater was. The first one to be killed was Ismet Berbataj [phoen], then Naim Kurmehaj lost his head, and after 18 or 19 people whose bodies were disrupted as a result of the explosion. Naim Kurmehaj was close to me. I also mentioned Dr. Bahri from Gjakove. This is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. My question was that you said that all the prison buildings were hit. You explained what happened just next to you, and you said that 19 persons were killed there, and you could not have known from that place how many more prisoners were killed in the buildings. And you know that the assistant warden was killed and that some prison guards and other employees at the prison were wounded, and you could not know how many more prisoners were killed; is that correct or is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: We could know it because Miki asked us how many people were killed, and some prisoners went and dug them outside of the ruins and put them on a tractor. That's the injured ones from the 19th of May. And the other ones, we took their corpses and covered them in a blanket and we also counted the numbers. Another important detail for this Court is we wrote down the names and surnames of every prisoner. We put this note at the pocket of each one of them, in their clothes or close to their bodies. This was simply done by your henchmen. I cannot even say your soldiers but your henchmen. They did this. And the reason why we did this note thing was because it was very important for their identification. And even today, for many of these people who were killed, their tombs are not known and their whereabouts are not known.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you can have ten minutes more, in the circumstances, which gives you a quarter of an hour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I don't even need 10 hours if this is the kind of answers he gives to my questions. You let him talk about anything that comes to his mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Mr. Milosevic, get on with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please. It says in your statement: "The bombing of the buildings continued for two or three hours. Aeroplanes were taking their turns in bombing the prison and firing rockets. When they would finish, they would fly away and other aircraft came in and continued the bombing. We remained in block C2 until night fell, and then we went to the sports field area where many other prisoners had gathered. Some prisoners here were hit and injured by bomb fragments that had come over the wall." And so on and so forth. Now, how should I put this, this main topic of yours? I am going to read out to you what you said yourself, but please answer the following question first: How many policemen, as you have been asserting, took part in this shooting at you while you were in that area, in this open area within the prison compound as you were lined up? Just give me the number, please, without any additional explanations.

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: I cannot say the number because -- well, simply, I could say approximately 20 persons based on the fact that on the 23rd of May when they gathered us, the same person with the same voice, except wearing a mask, was there when I had the honour, so to say, to be half a metre away from him. But I can say there were -- on the 23rd, there were 20 or 30 of them. But on the specific day, I could not say the exact number because they were on the watchtower and it was impossible for me to count. But on the 23rd, I can say there were 20 or 30 of them, wearing different uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm asking you about what you have to say to that. You say 20 or 30. Now, this is what you wrote here. They were shooting at you, right, from bazookas and automatic weapons on the external side. "Mortar projectiles were fired at us and rifle grenades." You say that you recognised the sound that can be heard in the air. And you say that they were shooting at you with automatic rifles, mortars across the wall, throwing hand grenades. And before that, they lined you up and they wanted to kill you. Is that your claim?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: You are confusing things on purpose because they did not fire with bazookas from behind the wall. It doesn't say bazooka in the statement. It means something similar to a bazooka, therefore, a Zolja. They shot with bazookas and then they were behind the wall. They threw the grenades over the wall and onto us, and they also fired through the hole in the wall with rifles, automatic guns, and other types of weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All right. Please let us try to clarify this entire story of yours now.

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: No. It's not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm saying that it is not a fairy tale. What you have been saying, your words are a fairy tale.

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: [In Serbian] But they're not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Both of you remember you're in a court, and this kind of argument is of no assistance at all. Mr. Cekaj, would you remember that you are answering questions to the Court and not arguing with this accused. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you describe the following event, and this happened according to what you said. You were lined up, they lined you up, and they carried out an execution; right? That's what you're claiming. They lined you up, executed you, and then you fled in different directions but you did not manage to run away altogether because you remained within the prison. And after that, they collected you and then they did not execute you but they put you on buses and trucks and more than 800 of you were taken to other prisons. Is that your story?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: The -- our lining up and execution has no other name but execution itself. And as how, who, why, and when is concerned, then you and your authorities would know better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But can you explain the following to me: What's the point of all of this, even if somebody did have this kind of idea, to line you up, to execute you, and then to transfer 800 of you to other prisons and to take the wounded to hospitals, take care of you, bring you food, bread, cigarettes, et cetera, after having executed you? What's the point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not a matter for him. You'll have to ask those who were responsible, Mr. Milosevic. I suppose you could put the question in this way: Could you see any point in what was happening? Could you understand any intention yourself or not, Mr. Cekaj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no logic in this. The only logic is that of people who are mentally sick and spiritually sick and who are filled with national hatred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Very well. Yes. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this cannot be explained because it's inexplicable, Mr. May. That's the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cekaj, since it is clear -- we saw a BBC film yesterday where the catastrophic effects can be seen of the bombing of the prison, even during the filming itself, there was a wave of bombing.

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: Ask the concrete question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And 92 corpses were taken out of the rubble. What you have been saying here, is that aimed at diminishing what NATO did by targeting the prison as a civilian target?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: I didn't see an actual question, however, I can also provide an answer to this confused question. As a result of the NATO bombing, 23 people died. The others were all dead because of the executions and basically as a result of merciless killings as if being in a blood-feud situation. This is my answer. If you do not like it, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that only 30 corpses were taken out, those that were killed of the so-called blast effect; without any external injuries, their lungs burst?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: Where were they found?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know or do you not know? Just give me a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: Where were these 30 bodies exhumed without any injuries? I only know that there were only two persons I saw. One of them who -- he had been hanged. Also there is a logical question that comes up; you are a lawyer and obviously you have been through the bar examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't argue with the witness -- with the accused. It's pointless. Mr. Milosevic, have you any other questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, because you were in prison at that time as well, that a team of the investigating judge from the court in Pec carried out an on-site investigation, that this investigation was interrupted and that it took place for several days, that all the corpses that were taken out were photographed, and that all the necessary elements envisaged by the investigation were registered, proper documents were supplied, and the effects of the NATO bombing were registered, the NATO bombing that took place day after day during those few days? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: Okay. A logical question: Where are the names of the identified bodies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Either you know or you don't know. If you don't know, Mr. Cekaj, just say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know. I know. A group of experts came. That was the way it was interpreted. They were military experts. Some of them were wearing uniforms. But they only came to see the damage caused by the NATO bombing in the objects. Therefore, only material damage. No question was raised as to human damage. This happened on the 19th of May, probably three or four hours after what happened happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that in addition to the presence of this investigation team that was working there and that was sent by the District Court in Pec, that there were many journalists from both home and abroad, and they took photographs of the killed and the injured and that there is a lot of proof in terms of what happened in the prison there?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: Obviously there are distorted proof, there is distorted evidence. There were some journalists from Belgrade there and a crew made of one or two persons, a reporter and a photographer from Greece. They were allowed there with your permission, and of course they construed the event in the way that it was more convenient for you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know how many of you prisoners from the prison in Dubrava were evacuated in order to be saved from further bombing? You were evacuated to other prisons. How many of you were evacuated?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: I did not count the prisoners that were left, but I think there were seven or eight buses and a truck. I know because I was in the first bus. I was in the third or fourth chair, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. A witness yesterday said that there were eight buses and four trucks. Tell me, do you know that about 800 prisoners were evacuated to other prisons then?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: I said I was in the bus -- I said I was in the first bus, maybe the third or fourth chair. And we were waiting in line. They took our clothes, our documents. They kept everything except for some valuables that we could keep by chance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has said he doesn't know how many prisoners were evacuated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, how come you had documents when you were in prison? When every prisoner is brought to prison, then his documents and personal belongings are taken away from him, everything that they are not allowed to keep in prison, even a belt, shoelaces, things like that. How come you had your documents in prison?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: The documents were composed of the papers on which -- papers about the detention and the imprisonment, but since it was a situation of anarchy and chaos, someone could found -- could manage to provide a belt for himself or shoelaces. But I know that someone would have trainers or leather jacket or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can you explain the following: You said just now that they forced you to leave your personal IDs, and now you say these documents that you received concerning your arrest, that you had only that. And it says here that you were supposed to leave your IDs. You could not have had your personal ID in prison.

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: I didn't say we had identification documents. You can ask them at the third floor of the state security building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this will have to be your last question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Xhemajli Sadik, a witness who was in prison with you, and he said yesterday that all of you had agreed amongst yourselves to destroy your documents so that somebody would not beat you in the prison in Nis. That was his explanation. Your explanation is to the contrary. Your claim is the documents were taken away from you. And on the third hand, so to speak, you could not have had any other documents except for these decisions that you refer to. So what is the truth in that respect and what is the truth at all?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. I've switched the microphone off. We'll pause. Yes, Mr. Cekaj. What is your explanation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The name of Sadik Xhemajli is unknown to me. I do not know this person. I have never heard of him before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Any questions from the amicus? Questioned by Mr. Kay:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some questions now about what happened when you were in prison, Mr. Cekaj. First of all, is it correct that you had white bed sheets whilst you were in there?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: For 18 months of my suffering, my sentence, 16 out of them I had not have white sheets and neither did I have a pillow. You can receive this -- you can obtain this information at the Red Cross Committee Centre. We had sheets in Pozharevc for two days because the Minister of Justice - Jankovic or something, I do not remember the exact name - came for a visit and they attempted to improve the situations. But shortly after that, I was released from prison in April of 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm looking at page 7 of the English version, in the middle of the page, fourth paragraph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it right that in the prison you used white bed sheets to form the word "SOS" in a place that aeroplanes would be able to see this signal?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: In block C2, there were no sheets. There were no pillows. The sheets that you are mentioning, we took them at the hospital, and we did -- we performed this action. There is another important fact: There were five or six trucks full of new mattresses stolen from the Divolli [phoen] company in Peja, bearing the company name. They were taken from the Keniu [phoen] Theatre. This is how we referred to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you make that signal with the white bed sheets to form the word "SOS" because you wanted the NATO pilots to see them and stop bombing the prison?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: Before this, the word written was "Help" in between blocks C1 and C2, because the field, the terrain was steep, therefore, the guards from the watchtower could not see it. We -- because they were under neon lights. However, we were aware of the danger and the risk we were running because if the guards would learn about it, we would risk our lives. We were careful to do this in places where the guards from the watchtower were unable to see it. But when they saw it eventually, they just destroyed it because they didn't know who had actually done it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you make these signals using the words "Help" and "SOS" because you hoped that the NATO pilots would see these signs and stop bombing?

utterances.speaker: MILAIM CEKAJ
utterances.text: Yes. This was on the 21st of May. That was the critical day of the bombardment. On the 22nd, the lining up and execution took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was going to ask a few questions about names of individuals that he remembers, however, I believe it's contained in his statement and I'll leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Cekaj, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. It was a pleasure to give my contribution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution will now call Mr. Ismet Haxhiavdija. And while we are waiting for this witness, Your Honour, if I may, just a few simple matters. I have prepared a brief summary of this witness's statement, which I would like to distribute to the Court, to the accused, and to the amici curiae. This witness, Your Honour, is an elderly man who suffers from diabetes, and because of that, his eyesight, particularly for reading, is not the best. So he may not be able to read the solemn declaration. It may be necessary for the Court or an officer to read the declaration to him. At the same time, because Mr. Haxhiavdija's name is not easy to spell, I have written it out in large letters, and with leave of the Court, I will ask that it be placed on the ELMO so that the public can see the correct spelling of the name. And, Your Honours, this witness's evidence will be relevant to page 10 of the Kosovo atlas, the town of Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, you can read out the declaration to the witness and it can be translated, can't it? I think that's the way we've done it in the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiavdija, would you mind standing, please. You're going to have the solemn declaration read to you. Would you repeat it after counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Haxhiavdija. Please repeat after me. Please repeat after me: "I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. If you'd like to sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Saxon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, is your name Ismet Haxhiavdija?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiavdija, were you born on the 10th of December, 1933?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you born in the city of Gjakove in Kosova?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiavdija, on the 9th of May in 2001, did you provide a statement to a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor about the events that you witnessed and experienced in Kosovo in 1999?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In January of this year, 2002, in the country where you now reside, did you have an opportunity to review a copy of the statement that you made in 2001 in the presence of a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor and a witness?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time, did you confirm that the copy that you reviewed was a true and accurate copy of the statement that you gave in May of 2001?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I will now offer that statement into evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis. And, Your Honours, I have taken the liberty of printing out a copy of this statement in extra large font for the benefit of this witness. So if this particular copy in large font be placed in front of him in case he needs to refer to it, I would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 298.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, Ismet Haxhiavdija is a Kosovo Albanian man, a Muslim, who was 65 years old when the events alleged in the indictment occurred. For many years, Ismet Haxhiavdija taught the Albanian language and literature in Kosova. He has four sons. Mr. Haxhiavdija describes how Serb forces began killing Kosovo Albanian residents of Gjakove and burning houses after the NATO bombing commenced in March 1999. On the morning of 2 April 1999, Mr. Haxhiavdija's son, Behar, came to his home. Behar told his father, "Father, my life is ended." Behar explained that his wife and five children had been killed the night before. Behar Haxhiavdija and other survivors left for Albania that same morning. Mr. Haxhiavdija decided to remain in Gjakove. The following day, Mr. Haxhiavdija went to the Vejsa family compound in order to try to recover the bodies of his daughter-in-law and his five grandchildren. Mr. Haxhiavdija did not enter the compound after he was warned that it could be dangerous to do so. Serb police and military were driving in the area. Mr. Haxhiavdija visited the office of the police that was responsible for the burial of bodies. Mr. Haxhiavdija knew the officer in charge of this office, and that officer sent several Roma employees to the Vejsa family compound to recover the bodies that were there. When he returned to the Vejsa family compound, Mr. Haxhiavdija saw the burned body of Hysen Gashi. Eventually, Mr. Haxhiavdija was told that there were many bodies inside the house. A total of 20 bodies were found in the rubble, 19 of them were women and children. The youngest victim was two years old. Mr. Haxhiavdija remained in Gjakove with his wife. Most of the time they stayed at a neighbour's home because they were afraid to remain alone. Several times during May 1999, Mr. Haxhiavdija watched as Serb policemen would enter homes and steal property of persons who had fled to Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll take the adjournment now before cross-examination. Mr. Haxhiavdija, we're going to adjourn now for 20 minutes. Could you be back then, please, to conclude your evidence, and could you remember in the adjournment --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include members of the Prosecution team. We will adjourn now for 20 minutes

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wondered whether I might just address you on a brief administrative matter, to give as much notice as possible. I seek the Court's permission to change the schedule of witnesses for tomorrow for the reason that I am available tomorrow to take some witnesses whom I've prepared and proofed and for whom witness summaries are available for distribution. They were planned to give evidence tomorrow. I am here tomorrow, but for -- I have other trial-related commitments elsewhere on Monday and will not be here when some of the witnesses would otherwise testify. So I'm asking, after this witness completes today, that's number 8 - we've already done number 9 - number 10, Mr. Pnishi, we may start this morning. I would then ask that when he finishes on Friday morning, I would ask that we skip number 11 and do number 12, Mr. Gani Beqaj, and number 14, Sofije Imeraj. Those are two witnesses that I personally would like to lead because I have proofed them. And then just revert back to number 11, 13. So that is my request, and I thought I should raise it now so that there's no suggestion that we're doing this at the very last moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Haxhiavdija, in your statement you say that the Albanians in Kosovo suffered reprisals for many years, and at the very beginning you say that you were not even allowed to sing your own songs. This, I suppose, refers to Albanian songs, does it not?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you not allowed to sing such songs?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Nowhere. Not even -- not just in schools but even in the streets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in which period? To what time period does this allegation apply when you were not allowed to sing Albanian songs?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: From the time of Rankovic and up including the time that you came to power with the exception of the years around 1974 when Kosova had -- was said to have a certain minimal autonomy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who prohibited singing of your songs?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Your regime. Your regime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the period that you mentioned, I was still at secondary school.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: I said the time of Rankovic. And you made the situation even worse than at the time of Rankovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know, Mr. Haxhiavdija, that throughout this period you're referring to there was free airing of radio and TV programmes in Albanian, with many features and contributions and programmes of Albanian music and Albanian songs? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: There was a very small number of songs and music, songs which didn't have anything to do with politics or with national feelings, or they were songs that were general songs that were in favour of Yugoslavia. It's not only the songs but lessons, teaching. They were very -- there were thousands of writers, Albanian writers, and we were only allowed to teach about four or five of them who had nothing to do with national feelings. Very few of them we were allowed to teach.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you say that you taught Albanian language and literature, and I have no doubts about that, do you really think that there were thousands of Albanian writers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think we're going to be assisted by this. No doubt it's a figure of speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true -- very well. A figure of speech. Is it true that in Kosovo and Metohija there were cassettes and records and CD disks with Albanian national music sold on the open market and that such music was performed at various celebrations and in restaurants and coffee-shops without any limitations throughout this period up until the war? Do you know that? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: I'm not someone who sits around in coffee-shops, but I would say that all the songs and dances and records, only the ones that passed your censorship authorities. Those which had a bit of national feeling in them, not only were the songs forbidden but the people who sang them put in prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Haxhiavdija. It's a good thing for everyone to hear this. But tell us one thing, as a teacher of language and literature, you retired in 1991. Where were you working before your retirement?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: I worked at an elementary school in Brekoc called Zeklus Marku [phoen], in Brekoc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from 1991 when you became a pensioner, who did you receive your pension from?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: From the money that I had put into the system for 35 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course every employed person pays a certain percentage of his earnings into the social security funds. So you received your pension from the state pension funds, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: But it was money that I put into the fund myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Like all the other citizens of Yugoslavia. Whoever works contributes to the pension funds. But let us move on. You say that as of 1981, the situation in Kosmet worsened; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. But even earlier, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So you mentioned 1981 when the situation worsened after the demonstrations for a Kosovo republic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: The students saw the injustices that were being committed by the Yugoslav system, by your system, and they were obliged to stand up and to demonstrate, to demand freedom and independence as citizens, as people and then as Albanians too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You say on page 2 of your statement, in paragraph 7, that the number of policemen in Djakovica increased rapidly, that policemen were coming from all parts of Yugoslavia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: That's true. When the emergency measures were introduced in Kosova against the Albanians who were unarmed and who were not protected by any country on earth, by anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you say that the police officers came from all parts of the country and not only from Serbia, and you mention that the government was introducing some sort of measures. Do you remember those measures in 1981? And you yourself say that the police came from Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia, Montenegro, and everywhere else, that those measures were introduced by the Presidency of the SFRY after your demonstrations and demands for a Kosovo republic. Is that correct, sir, Mr. Haxhiavdija?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: That's true. And the head of the Executive Council of Yugoslavia, as one would call it, was a representative -- was a representative of Bosnia. Unfortunately, I don't know his name any more. I used to know it. But when you get old, you start to forget things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me remind you. He was a Muslim from Bosnia. His name was Raif Dizdarevic, and he headed the Presidency at the time. Do you remember now?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I remember now. Raif Dizdarevic, that's right. He was head of the Executive Council of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But let us now move on to the main part of your statement. But before that, will you please answer this question: How is it that in your statement you did not mention with a single word the events having to do with very numerous terrorist activities by the KLA in the Djakovica area?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: If you ask me a question, I can give you an answer. What are you getting at? I don't really understand what you're getting at.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me be more specific. Do you know that only during 1998 and in the first three months of 1999 in your municipality, that is the municipality of Djakovica, the KLA killed 18 Albanian civilians, eight police officers, and 16 soldiers of the army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: I don't know of any case of the KLA killing anyone except in direct -- in the direct war situation, and I could not imagine that they would ever have done such a thing. It's possible that one of the Albanians who -- who betrayed his country and went over to your side, then of course it could be possible that something happened to him, one of the Albanians. It's possible. Because the KLA is an army which is born of the people, to defend the population against massacres and crimes and oppression which were committed on the part of your army, police, and paramilitaries under your orders, under the orders of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Haxhiavdija. Do you consider that the enemies of the Albanian people are those Albanians who, for instance, were employed by the state? Let me mention policemen, post officers, forestry workers, people working in a state-owned company. After all, you yourself were working for the state until 1991, and after which you retired and received a pension. So what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: All those who were influenced by your policies, members of the SPS, traitors, those who worked for your services, but those -- but there were, on the other hand, Albanians who were honest, who were working to earn their money to make a life. They were different. One example -- I can give you an example. There were 33 teachers in the Brekoc school. Two of them were Serbs who were born and raised in Kosova and who knew Albanian just as well as we did. But in order to placate them, we were forced to speak Serbian in meetings with them, although the vast majority of the people at the meetings were Albanians. And that applies to everywhere where there were Albanians. Albanians were forced quite often to speak Serbian, even though the local Serbs knew -- who were in the minority, knew Albanian. They grew up there. They had their families there. They were nourished on the bread of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Haxhiavdija. You taught in elementary school and I assume that you did your teaching in Albanian, is that right, all the way up to your retirement?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Yes; I'm Albanian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not denying the fact that you're Albanian, and I'm not denying the fact that you had the right to teach children in Albanian, because that is their constitutional right. I just want to have it established that you normally held your lectures in Albanian to the children that you were teaching and nobody prevented you from doing that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: That's right. No one stopped me because we were the people who took part in the Second World War and who won and who worked to be equal and not to be slaves, even under Rankovic and under your administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think you have pursued this point about education sufficiently. We are simply getting into a political argument, which is of no great assistance to us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us move on to this war. You say that NATO aircraft bombed during the night and you say throughout the night, as a matter of fact. What did they bomb and where, to the best of your knowledge, Mr. Haxhiavdija?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: They bombed the Yugoslav army and police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Please give me an answer to the following: On the basis of what do you claim that the Serbs, as you had put it, during the first night of the bombing killed a father and a son by the name of Zherka? Izet Hema --

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Zherka is his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I've mispronounced it and it's not perhaps written properly here. Did you see who killed these people?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Other members of their family and the neighbours said they were killed by the army and police and paramilitaries who were working with one another. Not only those people were killed but also Dr. Rahimi was killed, and the son of Xhamil Dula, Agim Dula, and the son of Sami Isufi. And even now we don't know where his body is or what has become of him, whether he was taken by the police or -- we don't know anything about his whereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who said to you that they were killed by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: People saw that. Other people saw that. Their family. The family members and the neighbours saw it. There are documents about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was the members of their families who told you that they were killed by the Serbs. Now, tell me, please, Mr. Haxhiavdija, is it correct that Cabrat, a part of town, was taken by the KLA and that at the beginning of April, from that part of town people were evacuated and sought shelter at the electrical engines factory? And these were Albanian civilians, mostly old people, women and children. There were 700 of them. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There are two questions there. Mr. Haxhiavdija, would you deal with these two questions. The first question was this: Was part of the town taken over by the KLA at the beginning of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not a politician. I don't know. But as to what the accused said, Milosevic said, they didn't go to take shelter at the electro-engineer factory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you help us, seriously, Mr. Haxhiavdija. It's not a political matter, it's a straightforward matter of fact: Did the KLA take part of the town or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not true. They were in Cabrat but nowhere else, as far as I know. But as I say, I'm not a person who is interested in politics a lot. I'm a family man. I'm only interested in my job and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're not being asked anything political at this stage. It's just what you know yourself as to what happened. The other question you were answering was that people were evacuated from part of town, and I think you were answering that when I interrupted you. Were Albanian people evacuated from part of town; civilians, women and children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No one left the city voluntarily. They were forced by Yugoslav forces, and in particular the Serb forces, police, army, and paramilitaries. They were forced to leave their homes and to leave for Albania. My neighbours, everyone in my neighbourhood, they were all forced to leave, to go into exile because they were in danger. In every second they could be killed, tortured, massacred. And there were thieves all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiavdija, a moment ago you said that in Cabrat there was KLA. So is it correct that Albanians, civilians, about 700 of them, mostly old people, women and children, were evacuated from Cabrat not under threats of the Serb army and police, as you had put it, but because this part of town was taken by the KLA? Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: No. The truth is that military forces and the police and the paramilitaries, the Serbian paramilitaries, not only forced the population to leave but massacred a fair proportion of our young people in the way that they know best. Because the KLA never threw people out of their own homes because the KLA came from these homes themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They fled in order to avoid combat operations, Mr. Haxhiavdija, because they were not expelled from Cabrat by any kind of police forces or military forces. You said yourself that the KLA was there. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: The KLA was only in the meadows of Cabrat, and the people who left were banished from their houses in Cabrat and in Buzh and other neighbourhoods of Gjakove. People entered these houses only for the purposes of violence and for the purposes of the Serbian police, army and paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's not waste too much time. Give me a specific answer to this question: Is it correct that from Cabrat - I hear it is called Cabrat now, and you know that better than I do - that from Cabrat, members of the KLA set out to launch an offensive towards the centre of town and the police station with the intention of taking the entire town. Are you aware of that, Mr. Haxhiavdija?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: That is not true. The truth is that on the 7th of May, 1999, the army, the police, and the paramilitaries attacked Cabrat and massacred these young men who were unarmed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that for a week at the beginning of April there was fierce fighting between the police and the brigade of the KLA and that the police had sustained losses then? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: And also, do you know that at that time the members of the KLA suffered heavy losses? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Inside the city of Gjakove, there was never any fighting. In the hills and in the south-west and the north-west, I'm not sure because I wasn't there. I'm an elderly man. If I had been a young man, I would have been there too. I would have put on a uniform and I would have gone out with the KLA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know -- or, rather, is it correct that throughout this fighting that you have been referring to as well, except that you say that this was around town rather than in town, that NATO incessantly and unselectively bombed Djakovica and even private houses were not spared?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I simply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Haxhiavdija. There's a point being made by counsel. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm just concerned, Your Honour, that the accused's question seems to put a twist on the prior response of this witness that is simply inaccurate. The witness has said that he was unaware of what was going on outside of the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Now, you can ask a question, if you want, about the bombing, Mr. Milosevic, but don't confuse the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiavdija, did you say that fighting was taking place in the hills, not in the centre of town? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: There was no fighting in the centre of town. The NATO bombing fell on the barracks and the police station to the south, and there was nothing to the north.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Haxhiavdija, you say that there was no fighting in the centre of town. The fighting between the police and the KLA, was that taking place in the hills rather than in the centre of town? Is that what you've been saying?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: It wasn't the KLA that attacked your army or police. You attacked Cabrat. You attacked the KLA in Cabrat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's leave aside who attacked who. Where were they fighting? In spite of who had attacked who, in which part of the territory was this fighting between them taking place?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Around Cabrat, in the western part of the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So while the fighting went on in that territory that you said, is it correct that during that fighting NATO bombed Djakovica? And not even private houses of Albanians were spared. As you know, they are the majority population of Djakovica. Is that right or is that not right, Mr. Haxhiavdija?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's dealt with the bombing. He said that they bombed the barracks and the police station to the south of the town. Now, if you're suggesting that's wrong, you should do so, but do it clearly so the witness can answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiavdija, is it your assertion that not a single NATO bomb fell on any private houses or other buildings or facilities in Djakovica? Is that your assertion?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: That's true, because they attacked only the barracks. And as evidence of this, the Catholic church was next door to the yard of the army barracks and not even a window was broken. It wasn't bombed. And there were no private houses bombed. And the same is true of the police station, which is on the road to Prizren. And there was only one road dividing the police station from private houses, and nothing happened to the private houses except for a shock and the earth shook when the police station was bombed. There was no damage from NATO bombing in the city itself. These towns suffered from the shelling of the Serbian forces. And you, as President of Serbia, had sent all kinds of criminals, all kinds of people without any kind of human feelings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiavdija, we understand your feelings, but you must just confine yourself to the evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiavdija, was any member of your family a member of the KLA, and if so, did any such people take part in the fighting that we referred to?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: I come from a large family, but none of our family was a member of the KLA. And I am a member of a family that always minded its own business, and we did our duty to the state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You say that your son Behar was trying to talk you into going to Albania, all of you, and that, apart from you and your other son Mendoh, everybody accepted that. Does that mean that you decided to go to Albania because the lives of your family members were not safe and that this was also because of the fighting in town and because of the bombing?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: My son suggested that I should go, and my third son, Mendoh, didn't go with my two big sons because on the road and at the border, you killed our young men. You have maltreated our young people. So the idea was that some of our family should remain alive. So he didn't go immediately. But after two days -- and he said, "Father, they're killing young people, so one of us should remain alive to keep the family going."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I asked you about when they were talking you into going to Albania. Was the motive for this proposal to go to Albania the lack of safety in Djakovica, the fighting that was going on and the bombing, that you should seek shelter from that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: They killed my daughter-in-law, three children, 13 children in the Vejsa house, six women, one of whom who was 80 years old, and you killed people, and you burnt the other members of the family, 20 of them. You have burnt a daughter who was mentally ill. So how should we not want to escape? We would go anywhere just to save our skins from the crimes and the massacres and the torture and the theft and the looting that was committed by the army, the paramilitaries, and the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Haxhiavdija. All right, Mr. Haxhiavdija. Let us stick to the questions that I am putting to you so that we don't waste any time, because these killings, massacres, tortures, et cetera, as you know, were carried out by the KLA in enormous numbers, but let us go back to what you have been claiming. According to the description of the Vejsa house that you give on page 3 in the first and first and fourth paragraphs, there was quite a bit of rubble in it. You did not see the bodies of the dead people, and they were underneath the rubble. Does all of this indicate that the Vejsa house had been hit by a bomb? You yourself stated that the body of Hysen Gashi was black because of the fire. So what you saw, what you described, doesn't all of that indicate that the house had actually been hit by a bomb? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: No. The Gashi house was built with two rooms and a corridor if you go adding from houses on the right. But the victims, these are children, were taken from the basement which was near the entrance, were taken 15 or 17 metres away to the flat where they lived, and there you massacred them and you burned them. You burned their house and the house roof was covered with tiles, and was also insulated by earth because of the heat. And all of these that I saw on the first day, that I couldn't tell the difference. And the workers from Cabrat organisation said that a crime had taken place in this house. And when I went back to my own house, these workers called for me to Cabrat and communicated to me the news that in that house where the bodies are, it is true that there are bodies, but we are scared to go there, and we are scared that you who have a heart condition might have a heart attack and might die when you see them. But there are bodies there. And the next day I went to bury them, and my son -- and my son said to me, "It's a sin to see your children like that." And the children, as I said before, there were 13 of them. And one of them belonged to my neighbour and he was 18 months old. Just imagine. Just see it. My grandson, my grandchild, four years old. Just imagine. With what kind of human feelings can somebody commit a crime of this kind against children, against old people, against young people who have never done a single thing? They didn't even have a knife to peel an apple let alone fighting against your forces, because you mobilised them a long time ago. And this was your fascist intentions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, have you got any more questions of this witness, given the condition which he's in?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do. I do have questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiavdija --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You do not have very long left, so bring it to a close fairly quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: War is a crime in itself, and it is the innocent who most often lose their lives during a war. Is it clear to you who had created this war, Mr. Haxhiavdija? You are furious because of the death of your family. Everybody would feel that way. But how come there came to be a war, Mr. Haxhiavdija?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: You are the one who caused the war. Your regime. You as President, and the Presidency of Serbia, by sending criminals, the most evil criminals to us to commit crimes against children in front of the eyes -- in the very eyes of their mothers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiavdija, that house of the Vejsa family, was it in Cabrat?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what I thought. So there was fighting, and they were in the Vejsa household to take shelter from the fighting. Isn't that so, Mr. Haxhiavdija?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you allow for the possibility, Mr. Haxhiavdija, that where there was fighting, that any side might have provoked the conflict in which your family members were killed? You didn't see the Serbs provoking that conflict, did you, Mr. Haxhiavdija?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: There was no conflict. There was my son there with four members of his family. The crime committed against that family, against other families, there was no fighting there. And the young sister-in-law had Serbian and Montenegrin neighbours, and they went to them and said that -- and they said that crimes are being committed against us, but these neighbours said no, we will protect you, we will look after you, but it seems that they themselves took part in these crimes against the Vejsa family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this must be your last question, given the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. If it is my last question, then I must leave out many questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But let me ask you this last one, Mr. Haxhiavdija: Is it true that it follows from your entire statement and from your testimony here in court that you personally, you personally - you, Ismet Haxhiavdija - did not see a single killing allegedly committed by the Serbian forces and that you are testifying about those killings on the basis of the stories told by other people, that is, from hearsay? Is that correct, Mr. Haxhiavdija?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: No, that's not true. I saw my son. His wife was killed, his children, friends. Thirteen children, tiny children. The smallest one was eight months old. Old woman, 80 years old. And another person, Hysen Gashi, whom I saw how he fell down, how he collapsed in the annex to the building where the massacre was committed. Twenty members of six families there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Have the amicus any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, may I say two words? May I say something of my own here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, but briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to thank The Hague Tribunal, Tribunal in The Hague, for the invitation. I normally couldn't be here because of my ill health, but I did want to make my statement in front of the Tribunal and in front of the world opinion about the crimes and the tortures and the massacres which were committed by the police and the Serb army and paramilitaries against old people, against children, against young people whom, as I said, didn't even have a razor or a knife to peel an apple. So I would like to ask the accused --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. I think --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- your feelings, do you have any feelings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We must bring this to a close. Yes. Mr. Saxon, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour, very briefly, on two points. Re-examined by Mr. Saxon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiavdija, the accused suggested to you that the Vejsa house might have been hit by a NATO bomb. My question for you, first of all: How far was the home where you were staying in Gjakove from the Vejsa house? Approximately how far?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: About one kilometre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And prior to the evening of the 1st and 2nd of April when NATO bombs fell in the area of Gjakove, did your house shake when the bombs fell?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Bombs fell on the military barracks to the south and then the house did shake. But when my family and in-laws were murdered, there was no shaking. When the police station was bombed - that was about two kilometres away - my house and the Vejsa house, they didn't suffer any damage at that moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiavdija, to your knowledge, did any NATO bombs fall on Gjakove on the night of the 1st and 2nd of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: No. There was no bombing at that time at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic also suggested that your family members may have died as a result of fighting in or around the house where they had taken shelter. When you went to retrieve the bodies of your family members, to your knowledge were the bodies of any KLA soldiers found in that compound?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: No. That's quite inconceivable. The UCK were around Cabrat. There was no place that the UCK could take up position or stay. And there was no bombing there; the house was burnt and the roof fell in, the ceiling fell in. And they covered everything, all the bodies, where there were 20 people inside there and in the annex of Hysen Gashi, as I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiavdija, approximately how far is the Cabrat neighbourhood from the Vejsa compound?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Cabrat to the Vejsa compound, about half a kilometre, I would think. Maybe 600, 700 metres, but approximately half a kilometre. Less than a kilometre, because the Vejsa house is near the bus station, and Cabrat is on the west side of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiavdija, thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give your evidence. It's now concluded. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution now calls Mr. Martin Pnishi. Your Honours, while we wait for the witness to arrive, for your reference, the events to be described occurred in Meja village, Gjakove municipality. And for your reference, the Kosovo atlas, that is on page 9, grid reference H21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat. Examined by Mr. Shin:

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to repeat the question: Witness, could you please tell the Court your first name and last name.

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: Yes. I am Martin Pnishi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Pnishi, were you born on 9th of March, 1944, in Ramoc village in the municipality of Gjakove, Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you, in the beginning of 1999, living in Meja village, also in the municipality of Gjakove?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Pnishi, on the 4th of April, 2000, did you give a statement to a member of the Office of the Prosecutor about the events you witnessed and your experiences in Kosovo during 1999?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the 14th of March, 2002, did you provide a short addendum do your statement of the 15th of April, 2000? I'm sorry, of the --

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a correction there; on the 4th of April, 2000, that earlier statement.

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Pnishi, also on the 14th of March, 2002, were you provided with a copy of the statement you had previously given and a copy of the addendum, both in the Albanian language, in the presence of a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor and a presiding officer appointed by the Registrar of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time, were you able to confirm that the copy of the statement and the addendum were true and correct to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Pnishi, on Tuesday the 27th of August, earlier this week and also this morning, while speaking with myself and other members of the Office of the Prosecutor, did you become aware that there were a few revisions and corrections to be made to your statements?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First, in your statement of the 4th of April, 2000, you state that -- and this is in the first paragraph of that statement, Your Honours. You state that you worked in 1999 as a farmer. What was your profession between 1969 and 1983?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: I was a traffic policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you based as a traffic police officer?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: Yes. In Rahovec, the municipality of Rahovec.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pnishi, you also say in that 4th of April, 2000, statement, in the course of describing two police officers approaching your house, that - and, Your Honours, I'm looking in the English, page 3, the second full paragraph: "They wore masks and green camouflage uniforms." Is that correct? And if not, could you make any corrections to that.

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: That's correct. No. The uniforms were blue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also on that statement -- and, Your Honours, I'm going to refer now to page 4 of this statement in English, the last partial paragraph. Mr. Pnishi, in that statement you mention that: "... on the 27th of April -- Tuesday, the 27th of April, the bodies were collected on the next Sunday, the 2nd of May." Is that date correct, the date upon which the bodies were collected?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: It should read "Saturday" not "Sunday."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that should read Saturday the 1st of May rather than Sunday, the 2nd May?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: Yes, Saturday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going to your statement from the 14th of March, earlier this year, Mr. Pnishi, you mention that a Hamdi Alitaj told you: "He said that on Sunday they had loaded 412 bodies on trucks and tractors." Mr. Pnishi, is that correct? And if not, could you please indicate what correction should be made.

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: No. They said that 412 people shot were put onto a truck. I saw the truck which went to Korenica. It was filled, and it returned to the village of Meja and then it loaded again and then it passed by my house, the tractor and a truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Pnishi, could you please indicate whether the date is correct. Was that a Sunday or was it some other day?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: It was a Saturday. It was a Saturday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Also on the 14th of March, 2002 statement, you state that: "Five days after the trucks were loaded with bodies, Hamdi Alitaj came to my house supposedly to ask for a scythe but I think that the Serbs sent him to find out if we were at home or not." Is the timing indicated in that sentence correct? And if not, could you please indicate when it was that Hamdi Alitaj did come to speak to you.

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
